intro.heading: Understand the device in the context of the procedure.
paragraphs: Our initial focus is endourology—a specialty where visualization, access, navigation, retrieval and drainage must function together inside tightly constrained anatomy.
We ask how devices fit, how they are handled, which procedural interfaces matter and what evidence is needed to support each claim.
Commercial product information is published only with verified supporting documentation. Investigational concepts remain clearly separated from clinical availability.

approach.heading: Clinical insight. Engineering discipline. Responsible commercialization.

model.heading: A focused portfolio with a separate innovation track.

segments.name: Biomaterial innovation
segments.subtitle: A hydrogel approach to residual stone-fragment retrieval.
segments.lead: We are developing an in-situ forming hydrogel intended to capture residual kidney-stone fragments and dust in a cohesive gel for basket-assisted endoscopic retrieval.
segments.meta: TORSH’s investigational in-situ forming hydrogel programme for residual kidney-stone fragment retrieval. Explore the proposed concept and development questions.

question.heading:
Can small fragments become
one retrievable collection?
paragraphs: That question guides our lead biomaterials programme. Instead of considering the fragment alone, the concept introduces a material intended to surround and hold residual stone fragments and dust.

The design objective is controlled delivery, formation of a cohesive gel around the material, and removal with endoscopic retrieval instruments. These are intended functions, not established clinical results.

segments.workflow_intro: A concept sequence—not instructions for clinical use. Delivery conditions and device compatibility remain part of development.

workflow.title: Deliver
workflow.text: Introduce the components at the intended site through an endoscopic delivery pathway.

workflow.title: Form & capture
workflow.text: Form a gel in situ, with the aim of incorporating residual fragments and dust into a cohesive collection.

workflow.title: Retrieve
workflow.text: Engage the gel with a retrieval basket and remove the captured material through the intended retrieval pathway.

segments.questions_heading: What the programme needs to establish
segments.questions_intro: The programme brings materials questions and procedural questions into the same development plan.

questions.title: Delivery & formation
questions.text: Can the components be delivered controllably, and can gel formation be managed under the intended procedural conditions?

questions.title: Capture & integrity
questions.text: Does the gel incorporate fragments and dust, remain cohesive during handling, and permit retrieval without unwanted breakup?

questions.title: Instrument compatibility
questions.text: How does the concept interact with the delivery channel, basket and retrieval pathway? Compatibility needs to be evaluated as a system.

questions.title: Safety & translation
questions.text: What biological-safety, sterilisation, stability, manufacturing and clinical evidence is required before the technology can be introduced?

segments.stage_text: The programme is undergoing further development and testing. Safety, clinical effectiveness and compatibility with specific instruments remain to be established. The technology is not offered for clinical use.
segments.collaboration_text: We are interested in clinical input on retrieval workflows, biomaterials and testing expertise, and manufacturing perspectives relevant to further development.

A short-lived one-way identifier derived from a request IP address may be used to limit automated form abuse; the public form does not display or retain the raw address in an enquiry record.

sections.heading: Product and research status

The biomaterials programme is investigational. Its proposed mechanism is not evidence of safety or clinical effectiveness, and the technology is not offered for clinical use. Website descriptions do not replace product-specific instructions or professional clinical judgement.

families.name: Single-Use Flexible Ureteroscopes
families.hero: Digital visualization designed around upper-tract access.
families.metaDescription: Explore single-use flexible ureteroscopes for endourology and the key considerations in visualization, working-channel access and system compatibility.
families.overview: Flexible ureteroscopy brings visualization and treatment instruments through the ureter into the renal collecting system. A single-use flexible ureteroscope is designed for one procedure and does not require the multi-cycle reprocessing programme associated with reusable scopes. Evaluation should nevertheless consider imaging performance, maneuverability, accessory compatibility, total procedural cost and the associated display platform.
families.why: The scope is only one component of retrograde intrarenal surgery (RIRS). Deflection characteristics under accessory loading, irrigation behaviour, distal-tip dimensions and usable working-channel space can affect how the entire system is assembled. Device selection should be based on the manufacturer’s actual technical information and the centre’s clinical workflow.
families.intendedContext: Flexible ureteroscopy for upper urinary-tract assessment and endoscopic stone-management procedures where the device is appropriately indicated.
selectionChecks: Distal tip and shaft diameter; working length; active deflection with and without tools
Working channel diameter and compatibility with laser fibres, guidewires and baskets
Image system, processor/monitor compatibility, capture capability and connectivity
Irrigation, flow and visibility considerations during instrument use
Sterility, packaging, expiry and disposal instructions for the exact model

faqs.question: Are all single-use ureteroscopes compatible with the same monitor?
faqs.answer: No. Processor, connector and software requirements vary. Confirm the approved system pairing for the selected model.

faqs.question: Does single-use automatically mean better outcomes?
faqs.answer: No. Single-use changes reprocessing and logistics requirements, but clinical performance depends on multiple variables and available evidence.

families.relatedText: Ureteral Access Sheaths; Stone Retrieval Baskets; Flexible Ureteroscopy workflow

families.name: Single-Use Flexible Cystoscopes
families.hero: Flexible cystoscopy with a workflow-aware perspective.
families.metaDescription: Explore single-use flexible cystoscopy devices and evaluation factors such as imaging platform, insertion dimensions and procedural compatibility.
families.overview: Flexible cystoscopy supports visualization of the urethra and urinary bladder in diagnostic and selected therapeutic settings. A single-use flexible cystoscope provides a one-procedure instrument pathway and avoids reuse-related reprocessing of the scope itself. Choice between single-use and reusable platforms should account for procedural volume, system compatibility, handling, image quality and local procurement practices.
families.why: The practical questions extend beyond image resolution. Teams should establish whether the device works with their display hardware, which accessories pass through its working channel, how it is packaged and labelled, and how it will be used within outpatient or operating-room workflows.
families.intendedContext: Diagnostic cystoscopy and compatible urological interventions, including selected stent-related assessments, only as specified in the model’s intended use.
selectionChecks: Insertion tube and distal-tip dimensions
Field of view, image output and lighting approach
Working channel size and instrument compatibility
Tip articulation, shaft handling and ergonomic requirements
Processor/monitor compatibility and sterile single-use labelling

faqs.question: Can a flexible cystoscope be used for every cystoscopic intervention?
faqs.answer: No. Indications, channel size and accessories differ by model and clinical procedure.

faqs.question: Is a processing system always included?
faqs.answer: No. Some single-use platforms require a dedicated processor or display that must be procured separately.

families.name: Ureteral Access Sheaths
families.hero: A consistent access pathway within a complex procedure.
families.seoTitle: Ureteral Access Sheaths for Endourology | TORSH
families.metaDescription: Explore standard ureteral access sheaths and the device characteristics relevant to flexible ureteroscopy and repeated instrument exchange.
families.overview: During selected ureteroscopic procedures, a ureteral access sheath can provide a passage for repeated scope insertion and withdrawal. Designs differ in inner and outer calibre, working length, dilator configuration, tip geometry, coating and radiopaque features. Device selection must account for anatomy and the potential for insertion-related ureteral injury.
families.why: A sheath changes the access and irrigation arrangement around the scope. The effect on outflow, fluid pressure and instrument exchange cannot be understood from sheath diameter alone. Appropriate sizing and insertion judgement remain clinical decisions.
families.intendedContext: Selected flexible ureteroscopy and retrograde intrarenal surgery workflows where a ureteral access sheath is judged appropriate.
selectionChecks: Internal/external French size, usable lumen and working length
Tip transition, dilator compatibility and radiopaque marking
Surface coating and handling requirements
Scope and instrument diameter fit; potential flow constraints
Package, single-use labelling and manufacturer-specific precautions

faqs.question: Is a ureteral access sheath necessary for every ureteroscopy?
faqs.answer: No. It is used selectively according to the clinical context and the operating surgeon’s judgement.

faqs.question: Does a larger sheath always improve the procedure?
faqs.answer: No. A larger calibre changes access and outflow but must be balanced against anatomy and the risk of ureteral injury.

families.relatedText: Single-Use Flexible Ureteroscopes; Suction-Enabled Access Sheaths

families.name: Suction-Enabled Ureteral Access Sheaths
families.hero: Considering access and aspiration as one system.
families.metaDescription: Understand suction-enabled ureteral access sheath systems, their role in fluid and debris management and the questions to verify before selection.
families.overview: Suction-enabled ureteral access sheaths combine a scope access pathway with an aspiration channel or connection intended to assist fluid and debris management during selected endoscopic procedures. Some market designs are flexible and navigable, often described as FANS; not every suction sheath has those characteristics. Device-specific construction and intended use determine the correct terminology.
families.why: Aspiration cannot be evaluated independently of irrigation inflow, suction settings, ureteroscope dimensions and the surrounding renal anatomy. Clinical literature discusses intrarenal pressure, visualization and fragment evacuation, but a given device’s performance must be supported by its own evidence and instructions. TORSH will avoid outcome claims unless supported by the exact product and applicable evidence.
families.intendedContext: Selected upper-tract endoscopic stone-management workflows where a compatible suction access system is appropriately indicated.
selectionChecks: Standard suction sheath versus flexible/navigable design: confirm actual model
Suction port, tubing connection and compatible negative-pressure controls
Sheath dimensions, length and scope compatibility
Irrigation–aspiration balance and device-specific instructions
Evidence supporting any claimed pressure, visibility or fragment-clearance effect

faqs.question: Are suction access sheaths and FANS the same thing?
faqs.answer: Not always. FANS refers to a flexible and navigable suction access sheath; a conventional suction sheath may not navigate in the same way.

faqs.question: Can the website claim reduced infection or guaranteed stone clearance?
faqs.answer: No. Such claims require device-specific clinical substantiation and regulatory review.

families.relatedText: Ureteral Access Sheaths; Flexible Ureteroscopy workflow; Residual fragments insight

families.name: Nitinol Stone Retrieval Baskets
families.hero: Stone capture depends on access, geometry and control.
families.metaDescription: Explore endoscopic stone retrieval basket concepts and selection factors including basket architecture, diameter, tip configuration and channel fit.
families.overview: Stone retrieval baskets are designed to capture and manipulate selected urinary stone fragments during endoscopic procedures. Nitinol is used in many basket designs because of its elastic recovery and ability to form flexible wire structures. Tipless, tipped and other basket geometries serve different handling requirements; device characteristics and surgeon preference matter.
families.why: Retrieval instruments pass through limited working-channel space while the scope may be deflected. The basket’s outer diameter, opening configuration, wire arrangement and handle mechanics should therefore be considered alongside the scope, fragment size and access route.
families.intendedContext: Endoscopic stone capture, manipulation and retrieval in appropriate URS/RIRS or other labelled urological procedures.
selectionChecks: Basket design and available opening diameter
Tipless versus tipped configuration and retrieval strategy
Shaft diameter in Fr, working length and channel fit
Handle control and release behaviour
Sterile packaging, single-use status and IFU precautions

faqs.question: Is one basket shape ideal for every fragment?
faqs.answer: No. Basket geometry, stone size/location and endoscopic access influence device selection.

faqs.question: Does “nitinol” specify the whole device design?
faqs.answer: No. It identifies a material used in the basket; tip, shaft, wire pattern and handle still vary.

families.relatedText: Single-Use Flexible Ureteroscopes; Ureteral Access Sheaths; Stone-management workflow

families.name: Urology Guidewires
families.hero: The access pathway begins with the wire.
families.seoTitle: Urology Guidewires for URS & RIRS | TORSH
families.metaDescription: Learn about urology guidewires and how coating, core support, tip profile, length and diameter influence endoscopic workflows.
families.overview: Guidewires support access, navigation and exchange of instruments during urological procedures. Hydrophilic, PTFE-coated and hybrid configurations provide different handling characteristics. The appropriate combination depends on anatomy, procedure, compatibility and the intended balance between a low-friction distal segment and support along the shaft.
families.why: A guidewire is an interface product. Its tip shape, coating behaviour, core stiffness, torque transfer, diameter and length may affect compatibility with dilators, sheaths, catheters and stent delivery devices. No single coating or construction should be described as universally superior.
families.intendedContext: Selected ureteroscopy, retrograde intrarenal surgery, stent-placement and other urological access workflows according to device labelling.
selectionChecks: Wire diameter and length; straight versus angled tip
Hydrophilic, PTFE-coated or hybrid surface characteristics
Tip softness, support and torque characteristics
Compatibility with dilators, access sheaths and stent delivery systems
Sterility and the model’s handling and preparation instructions

faqs.question: What distinguishes a hydrophilic wire from a PTFE-coated wire?
faqs.answer: The surface coatings alter friction and handling characteristics; device performance also depends on the core, tip and intended use.

faqs.question: Can guidewires be selected by diameter alone?
faqs.answer: No. Length, shaft support, tip design, coating and device-system compatibility also matter.

families.name: Double-J Ureteral Stents
families.hero: Drainage devices require careful model-specific selection.
families.metaDescription: Explore Double-J ureteral stent categories and the key questions about material, dimensions, configuration and intended dwell time.
families.overview: A Double-J (DJ) ureteral stent is a tubular device placed to facilitate internal drainage between the renal collecting system and urinary bladder in selected clinical circumstances. Curled ends help maintain position. Common construction options across the market include polyurethane-based and silicone stents, but materials and coatings must be verified for the actual device model.
families.why: Stent selection is not defined by size alone. Material, diameter, length, visibility, tip and side-hole configuration, placement accessories and labelled maximum indwelling duration may all affect the procurement specification. Patient experience and complication risks remain clinical considerations rather than marketing promises.
families.intendedContext: Internal ureteral drainage where a treating clinician determines stenting is appropriate and the selected stent’s label supports the intended use.
selectionChecks: Diameter, length, pigtail configuration and open/closed ends
Polymer formulation and coatings documented for the actual SKU
Radiopaque features and placement accessory compatibility
Sterile package, supplied components and traceability
Manufacturer-labelled maximum dwell time and follow-up instructions

faqs.question: Are silicone and polyurethane ureteral stents interchangeable?
faqs.answer: No. Different materials and designs have distinct handling and performance characteristics; selection should reflect the actual model and clinical requirements.

faqs.question: Can the website suggest an indwelling duration?
faqs.answer: Only by quoting the approved, model-specific IFU; do not apply a generic duration to the entire category.

solutions.metaDescription: Understand the device interfaces within flexible ureteroscopy and retrograde intrarenal surgery, from access and visualization to fragment management.
solutions.h1: Flexible ureteroscopy is a system, not a single instrument.
body: Retrograde intrarenal surgery (RIRS) uses a flexible ureteroscope to access the upper urinary tract and, where indicated, support endoscopic stone management. A procedural setup may involve imaging hardware, guidewires, access sheaths, laser fibres, retrieval baskets, irrigation arrangements and ureteral stents. Each component affects the usability of others.

When discussing devices for flexible ureteroscopy, TORSH focuses on the fit between scope and working-channel accessories, the choice of access system, imaging connections, irrigation and outflow, and retrieval needs. The balance among these elements is procedure- and patient-specific. Device specifications and the surgical team’s judgement remain central.

solutions.metaDescription: Explore flexible cystoscopy system considerations, including imaging, handling, working channels and stent-related procedures.
solutions.h1: Device selection for flexible cystoscopy starts with the clinical task.
body: Flexible cystoscopy is used to inspect the urethra and bladder and may support selected instrument-assisted procedures when the device is appropriately indicated. A cystoscopy platform comprises more than the scope itself: visualization hardware, working-channel accessories, handling and clinical workflow all shape its practical fit.

TORSH’s cystoscopy focus highlights compatibility, single-use logistics and responsible procurement evaluation. Hospitals should confirm the labelled clinical applications, actual device dimensions, accessories, imaging outputs and applicable reprocessing or disposal instructions for any device under consideration.
solutions.relatedText: Single-use flexible cystoscopes; Double-J ureteral stents

solutions.metaDescription: A procedure-led overview of endourology device functions: visualization, access, navigation, fragmentation interfaces and stone retrieval.
solutions.h1: From access to retrieval: understanding the full device pathway.
body: Endoscopic stone treatment involves multiple procedural decisions and device interfaces. Visualization provides anatomical orientation. Guidewires and access systems establish routes for instruments. Laser-based fragmentation requires a compatible delivery interface and appropriate fluid management. Baskets or other methods may be used for selected fragment retrieval; drainage devices may be indicated after treatment.

Product evaluation is therefore most useful when the complete workflow is considered. TORSH approaches stone-management technology by connecting real clinical tasks to the device characteristics that influence those tasks—while keeping performance claims separate from technical design intentions.
solutions.relatedText: Ureteroscopes; access and suction sheaths; retrieval baskets; guidewires; DJ stents

insights.title: Endourology Insights & Device Guides | TORSH
insights.meta: Read TORSH insights on flexible ureteroscopy, urology devices, access systems, stone retrieval, guidewires and translational device research.
insights.heading: Insights
insights.lead: A practical resource for the technologies that support endourology. We examine device families, system compatibility, procurement questions and the engineering challenges behind modern surgical workflows.
insights.disclaimer: Educational content only. Articles are not instructions for clinical use, medical advice or product-performance claims. Clinical review is required before public editorial release.

articles.seoTitle: Flexible Ureteroscopy: Understanding the Device System | TORSH
articles.metaDescription: A clinician-oriented overview of the device interfaces used in flexible ureteroscopy, from visualization and access to retrieval and drainage.
articles.excerpt: Flexible ureteroscopy is a coordinated workflow. Understanding how devices interact is often more useful than comparing any one feature in isolation.
articles.title: Understanding the Device Ecosystem in Flexible Ureteroscopy

sections.heading: A procedure made possible by interfaces
paragraphs: Flexible ureteroscopy is frequently described through the scope used to reach the renal collecting system. In practice, the scope is part of a larger technical arrangement. Visualization, entry, navigation, irrigation, stone treatment, retrieval and drainage each introduce constraints, and the success of a procedure cannot be reduced to one component. For a hospital evaluating endourology technologies, mapping those interfaces is a useful starting point.

sections.heading: Visualization and usable working space
paragraphs: Image quality matters, but so do the size and flexibility of the ureteroscope, its articulation in a deflected position, and what happens when a device is placed through the working channel. An image processor, connector and display may be model-specific. The procurement team should therefore ask about the full imaging system and the conditions under which advertised performance was measured.

sections.heading: Access changes the operating environment
paragraphs: Guidewires and ureteral access sheaths can assist navigation and instrument exchange in selected procedures. Sheath dimensions also influence the space available for irrigation outflow, and the act of placing a sheath introduces its own considerations. Suction-enabled variants add another interface: the balance between inflow, outflow and applied aspiration. Published literature is evolving, and model-level documentation remains essential.

sections.heading: Fragmentation is not the end of stone management
paragraphs: Laser fragmentation may generate a range of stone particle sizes. Depending on the case, surgeons may use baskets, suction-related arrangements or other approaches to manage fragments. Retrieval basket size and design must fit the working channel and the intended manoeuvre. Residual fragments remain a recognised post-treatment issue, so the distinction between device design intention and demonstrated clinical effect should be explicit.

sections.heading: A better way to compare technology
paragraphs: Rather than asking only which scope is “best”, begin with a device map: scope and processor; access and guidewire; laser fibre compatibility; irrigation and aspiration; retrieval accessories; and the drainage pathway when indicated. This reduces the risk of selecting individually attractive components that work poorly together. The manufacturer’s instructions for use and clinician judgement remain the final reference for safe use.

articles.editorialReferences: EAU 2026 Urolithiasis guideline [C1]; Advin directory was used only for topic taxonomy [A1].

articles.seoTitle: How to Evaluate Single-Use Flexible Ureteroscopes | TORSH
articles.metaDescription: A practical checklist for hospitals assessing single-use ureteroscope platforms, working-channel compatibility, deflection, handling and logistics.
articles.excerpt: Scope evaluation should cover articulation, instrument compatibility and the whole imaging system—not a headline camera specification alone.
articles.title: How to Evaluate a Single-Use Flexible Ureteroscope Beyond Image Quality

sections.heading: Start with the use case, not the product sheet
paragraphs: Single-use flexible ureteroscopes have changed how many centres think about device availability and reprocessing. A one-procedure instrument can remove the need to reprocess that scope, but this does not make all platforms technically equivalent. Case mix, procedure volume, compatible accessories, staffing and total ownership or per-case costs all influence the choice.

sections.heading: Evaluate visualization under realistic conditions
paragraphs: A high-resolution promotional image may not reflect the working view when the device is deflected, irrigation conditions change or a treatment accessory occupies the channel. Ask for information on image processing, field of view and the complete processor–monitor arrangement. A trial evaluation should use the actual setup proposed for procurement, with manufacturer-supported configurations.

sections.heading: Deflection and the working channel are connected
paragraphs: Articulation affects access within the collecting system. The range available without a tool can be different from the range obtained with a basket or laser fibre loaded. Likewise, two devices with similar external dimensions may differ in their usable channel capacity. A useful comparison includes distal-tip dimensions, shaft characteristics, loaded and unloaded deflection, and the intended accessories.

sections.heading: Single-use affects operations as well as instruments
paragraphs: Single-use systems reduce the reusable scope’s cleaning and reprocessing workload, while introducing other logistical issues: sterile stock, expiry management, packaging waste, compatibility of displays and responsible disposal. Real-world value depends on reliable availability, training and clear ownership of the full platform. Neither reusability nor disposability alone proves better patient outcomes.

sections.heading: Questions to ask a supplier
paragraphs: Request the approved intended use, technical sheet and instructions for use. Confirm the processor, display and connectors; the compatible channel accessories; packaging and expiry; servicing requirements for non-disposable hardware; and local regulatory and procurement documentation. A clear response to these questions is more useful than an unsupported claim of superiority.

articles.editorialReferences: Advin flexible disposable ureteroscope category [A3]; EAU 2026 Urolithiasis guidance [C1].

articles.seoTitle: Standard vs Suction Ureteral Access Sheaths | TORSH
articles.metaDescription: Understand the differences between conventional and suction-enabled ureteral access sheaths and the device-level questions that matter.
articles.excerpt: Adding aspiration changes the access system. It also changes which technical variables need to be verified.
articles.title: Standard vs Suction-Enabled Ureteral Access Sheaths: What Changes?

sections.heading: The conventional access pathway
paragraphs: A ureteral access sheath is used in selected ureteroscopic procedures to provide a route for repeated upper-tract access. Its inner and outer calibres, working length, dilator, tip transition and coating influence the device’s practical fit. The sheath can facilitate instrument exchange, but insertion-related ureteral injury remains an important consideration. It should not be presented as mandatory for every procedure.

sections.heading: What suction adds
paragraphs: Suction-enabled sheath designs introduce an aspiration route intended to assist evacuation of irrigation fluid and, depending on design, selected debris or fragments. This may be relevant to fluid management and visualization. The effect depends on the size and shape of the available outflow path, scope position, irrigation rate, suction settings and the patient’s anatomy. A “suction” label does not establish how one product performs.

sections.heading: FANS is a specific description
paragraphs: Flexible and navigable suction ureteral access sheaths are often abbreviated FANS. The term is not synonymous with every suction-enabled sheath. Some products remain relatively fixed in position; others are engineered to navigate further. Comparisons must identify the exact model, construction, intended use and operating conditions instead of treating all suction devices as a single class.

sections.heading: Clinical literature requires careful translation
paragraphs: The European Association of Urology discusses the influence of outflow, suction and ureteral access systems on intra-renal pressure and irrigation dynamics. That broader discussion does not authorise claims that any particular marketed device prevents complications, reduces urosepsis or guarantees better stone clearance. Such claims need direct model-specific substantiation and an appropriate regulatory basis.

sections.heading: A procurement checklist
paragraphs: Before evaluating a suction platform, request sheath and dilator sizes, length, suction-port geometry, tubing connections, compatible negative-pressure sources, device instructions and related evidence. Compare the complete operating arrangement, including scope and irrigation setup. Asking how a device manages trade-offs is usually more informative than asking for the strongest claim.

articles.editorialReferences: EAU 2026 Urolithiasis guidance [C1]; Advin standard and suction UAS product category pages [A5, A6].

articles.seoTitle: Stone Retrieval Baskets: Selection Considerations | TORSH
articles.metaDescription: Understand stone retrieval basket selection in URS and RIRS, including nitinol, basket shape, working-channel fit and fragment capture.
articles.excerpt: Basket geometry, working-channel compatibility and operator control determine whether a retrieval instrument suits the intended manoeuvre.
articles.title: Stone Retrieval Baskets: Matching Instrument Design to the Procedure

sections.heading: Retrieval begins before the basket opens
paragraphs: In ureteroscopy, stone retrieval is not only about whether an instrument can surround a fragment. The surgeon must first reach the intended area while preserving visualization and maneuverability. A basket moving through a flexible ureteroscope can influence deflection, irrigation and accessory handling. These practical constraints deserve attention during purchasing and testing.

sections.heading: Why nitinol is widely used
paragraphs: Nitinol can recover its shape after elastic deformation, which makes it useful for fine, flexible wire structures. But material alone does not determine performance. Wire arrangement, shaft properties, opening diameter, tip architecture and handle mechanics remain important. A basket may be described as tipless or tipped, and each design reflects particular access and capture trade-offs.

sections.heading: Think in terms of the fragment and the route
paragraphs: The dimensions and location of the fragment, intended capture technique and path of extraction shape basket selection. A large opening can be useful in one context and cumbersome in another. A small shaft might preserve working-channel space but is not necessarily appropriate for every loading requirement. Actual product indications and manufacturer limitations must guide use.

sections.heading: Compare with the ureteroscope, not beside it
paragraphs: A sound evaluation checks French size, working length, basket opening, tip and handle characteristics against the chosen ureteroscope and access sheath. Supplier demonstrations should use compatible systems, and any claims about strength or retrieval performance need product-level test support.

sections.heading: Procurement questions worth asking
paragraphs: Is the intended use stone extraction or another type of retrieval? Is the design tipped or tipless? Can the handle release a difficult capture? What channels and scopes are compatible? What sterile packaging and traceability accompany each unit? These questions create a practical description of the product without resorting to unsupported guarantees.

articles.editorialReferences: Advin stone basket directory [A7]; EAU 2026 Urolithiasis guidance [C1].

articles.seoTitle: Urology Guidewires & Double-J Stents: Key Questions | TORSH
articles.metaDescription: Explore how guidewire design and ureteral stent configuration influence device-system compatibility and endourology procurement.
articles.excerpt: Navigation and drainage devices may look familiar, but their material and configuration details are rarely interchangeable.
articles.title: Guidewires and Double-J Stents: Small Devices, Important Interfaces

sections.heading: The wire is a system component
paragraphs: Guidewires create a route for other devices, but their characteristics are not captured by diameter alone. Coatings influence surface friction. Core structure contributes to support and torque response. Tip shape, stiffness distribution and length can affect compatibility with dilators, catheters, sheaths and stent delivery devices. Different procedures may call for different combinations of these characteristics.

sections.heading: Hydrophilic and PTFE-coated designs
paragraphs: Hydrophilic coatings can be useful where low-friction navigation is desired, while PTFE-coated and hybrid designs may serve different handling or support preferences. Descriptions such as “atraumatic” or “superior trackability” should not be used as generic promises. The actual product design, device instructions and clinical context matter.

sections.heading: Drainage begins with an indication
paragraphs: A Double-J ureteral stent is used in selected situations to provide an internal drainage path from kidney to bladder. It does not need to be placed after every uncomplicated ureteroscopic procedure. Clinical judgement, procedural findings and current guidance determine when stenting is appropriate; a marketing page should not imply otherwise.

sections.heading: Stent configuration matters
paragraphs: Length, diameter, polymer formulation, curled ends, radiopacity, supplied accessories and labelled dwell duration vary among stent products. Silicone and polyurethane stents may differ in their handling and other characteristics. Hospitals need a model-specific specification and a process to track placement and planned removal, not generic assertions of patient comfort or encrustation resistance.

sections.heading: Build a compatibility checklist
paragraphs: Ask suppliers for approved instructions for use, wire and stent variants, sterile packaging, delivery-system details and applicable regulatory documentation. For a procedure involving both wire and stent, confirm the combination intended by the treating team. This is an example of why device procurement should be approached as a coordinated workflow.

articles.editorialReferences: Advin guidewire directory [A8] and DJ stent page [A9]; EAU 2026 guidance [C1].

articles.seoTitle: Residual Stone Fragments After RIRS | TORSH Insights
articles.metaDescription: Why small residual stone fragments remain an important endourology design problem, and what new retrieval approaches must demonstrate.
articles.excerpt: Stone fragmentation and complete fragment management are different challenges, creating an opportunity for carefully validated innovation.
articles.title: Residual Stone Fragments After RIRS: An Unfinished Engineering Question

sections.heading: Progress in fragmentation does not end the problem
paragraphs: Flexible ureteroscopy and modern laser systems have expanded the options for treating urinary stones. Nevertheless, the final state after fragmentation can include dust and small residual fragments. The ability to create smaller particles should not be confused with guaranteed complete stone clearance. Clinical follow-up and the significance of residual material depend on factors such as fragment size, composition and patient context.

sections.heading: Why residual fragments matter
paragraphs: Guidelines recognise that residual fragments may be associated with subsequent events or further intervention, while some fragments pass without incident. Their clinical importance is not uniform. This is precisely why technology developers should avoid selecting a single convenient endpoint as proof of value: retrieval rate, device usability, residual burden, procedure time and adverse events answer different questions.

sections.heading: Existing approaches have trade-offs
paragraphs: Baskets capture selected discrete fragments but occupy working-channel space and involve repeated manoeuvres. Dusting strategies may rely on later passage of fine particles. Irrigation and suction arrangements can influence fluid and debris movement, while the safe balance of pressure and visibility remains important. No one approach removes the need for procedure-specific judgement.

sections.heading: What a new retrieval technology would need to prove
paragraphs: An investigational approach intended to gather small fragments would need to demonstrate that it can be delivered through existing instruments, interact predictably with the operative environment, retain material during extraction, and be removed without unacceptable tissue or device-related risk. Bench performance is only an early part of that evidence. Biocompatibility, stability, sterility, usability, preclinical evaluation and any required clinical investigation must follow the relevant development pathway.

sections.heading: An engineering challenge, not a product promise
paragraphs: TORSH is exploring a biomaterial-based concept in this area. It remains investigational and is not available for clinical use. We view residual-fragment management as an example of the need for close dialogue between surgical teams, biomaterials researchers and device engineers—especially when technical feasibility must eventually meet clinical and regulatory standards.

articles.editorialReferences: EAU 2026 Urolithiasis guidance on residual fragments [C1].
